meta.name: Greyhound
meta.tagline: The world's fastest dog spends 18 hours a day on the couch — and turns out to be one of the best apartment dogs you can own.
meta.excerpt: Greyhounds are the great misconception of the dog world: built for 45 mph but content with a quiet apartment and a couple of daily walks. If you're open to adopting a retired racer, you may find the easiest large dog you've ever owned.
meta.meta_description: Greyhound owner's guide: temperament, exercise needs, health issues, adoption from racing rescue, costs, and whether a Greyhound fits your home and lifestyle.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Greyhound?
intro.html:
Greyhounds are the oldest purebred dog type in recorded history — depicted in Egyptian tomb paintings and mentioned in Greek literature. They were built for one purpose: explosive short-distance speed. A Greyhound can hit 45 mph in three strides. They are, by almost any measure, the most aerodynamically efficient land animal on earth relative to their body size.

And then they come home and sleep for 18 hours. This is the great paradox of the breed, and it's the reason Greyhounds work in apartments and smaller homes in a way that surprises everyone who expects an endurance athlete. They sprint, and then they're done. Their "off" switch is remarkably well developed.

Most Greyhounds available for adoption are retired racing dogs — typically 2–5 years old, already leash-trained, crate-trained, and mannerly. Greyhound adoption organizations have refined the transition process to the point where it's genuinely smooth for most families.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: What Greyhounds Look Like
appearance.html:
The Greyhound's physique is unmistakable: a narrow, aerodynamic head, deep chest, tucked abdomen, long muscular legs, and a lean, almost architectural body. Their skin is thin and their coat is short, smooth, and comes in nearly every color — fawn, brindle, black, blue, white, red, and combinations of each.

They have almost no body fat, which matters practically: they get cold easily and need a coat in winter, and they can't lie on hard surfaces for long without pressure sores. A good dog bed isn't optional — it's a health requirement for a dog with this little padding. They look elegant and delicate, but their muscle mass is extraordinary. Pick one up and you'll be surprised how heavy 65 lbs of pure muscle actually feels.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: Temperament
temperament.html:
Greyhounds are gentle, quiet, and surprisingly sensitive. They tend to be reserved with strangers but not fearful, and they warm up steadily over weeks and months. They're not the effusive, tail-whacking greeters that Labradors are — they're more dignified about affection, but it's real when it comes. Many Greyhound owners describe them as cat-like in their self-possession.

The two temperament traits that matter most practically: they have a strong prey drive, and they're sensitive to harsh handling. Sighthounds chase moving things — small dogs, cats, squirrels, cyclists. Whether a particular Greyhound can live with cats requires an individual assessment; many do fine, many don't. Responsible adoption organizations test this before placement.

They respond to calm, positive handling and do not do well with corrections or raised voices. They're not the most obedient breed — they'll look at you when you call, consider it, and decide based on what else is happening — but they're manageable and not difficult to live with.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Greyhound
mikes_take.html:
The Greyhound is one of the most underrated breeds for people who want a large, calm dog that doesn't need two hours of exercise a day. Two good walks and a couple of brief off-leash sprints in a securely fenced space are genuinely enough. They're quiet — not prone to barking. They don't chew things compulsively. They don't demand constant stimulation. They'll just be there with you, which is its own kind of wonderful.

The non-negotiable: you cannot let a Greyhound off-leash outside of a fully enclosed area. Their prey drive and speed together mean that once they spot something and run, they're gone — and they have no road sense. This is not trainable away. Every single Greyhound owner will tell you this. It's fencing or a leash, always, outside.

The other thing worth knowing: retired racers have often never climbed stairs, seen a mirror, been in a house, or navigated a slippery floor. The first few weeks involve a lot of "this dog has never encountered a glass door" moments. It's actually charming, and the adoption organizations prepare you for it. Within a month, most Greyhounds settle in as if they've always lived there.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: Care Requirements
care.html:
Exercise

Two 20-minute walks daily, plus the opportunity to sprint in a safely fenced area a few times per week. That's genuinely it. They're sprinters, not endurance athletes — a 5-mile run would exhaust and stress them in a way a quick burst doesn't. Never exercise heavily in heat; their thin skin and low body fat make them vulnerable to overheating.

Grooming

  • Brushing: Once a week with a soft brush or grooming mitt — minimal shedding
  • Bathing: Every 6–8 weeks; they're naturally low-odor
  • Teeth: Daily brushing recommended — Greyhounds are prone to dental disease
  • Nails: Every 3–4 weeks; nails grow fast on athletic breeds
  • Winter coat: Required in cold climates — they have no insulating undercoat

Sleeping

A thick, padded dog bed is a genuine health requirement — not a luxury. Without adequate padding, their bony prominences develop pressure sores quickly. Many Greyhound owners use orthopedic foam beds or even a dedicated couch spot.

I put together a full Greyhound grooming guide with the specific tools and routine that work best for this coat type.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: Health & Common Conditions
health.html:
Greyhounds are one of the healthier large breeds — they don't have the hip dysplasia prevalence of Labradors or the cardiac issues of Cavaliers. Their structural health vulnerabilities are specific and largely manageable.

ConditionWhat to Know
Dental DiseaseThe #1 health issue in the breed. Greyhounds have crowded, thin-enameled teeth that develop tartar and periodontal disease unusually fast. Daily brushing and professional cleanings every 1–2 years are standard for this breed.
Anesthesia SensitivityCritical: Greyhounds metabolize barbiturate-based anesthetics differently due to low body fat and liver enzyme differences. Any vet treating your Greyhound must know this. Most use propofol-based protocols instead. Inform every vet and emergency clinic.
Bloat (GDV)Deep-chested breeds are at higher risk. Feed two meals daily, avoid exercise 1–2 hours before and after eating, and know the symptoms: distended abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness. GDV is a surgical emergency.
OsteosarcomaBone cancer affects large breeds at higher rates. Greyhounds are not more prone than other large breeds, but it's worth knowing in the context of any limb lameness in older dogs.
Pressure SoresResult from lying on hard surfaces. Preventable with adequate bedding. Check elbows and hips regularly.

Important: Always carry a card noting Greyhound anesthesia sensitivity to any veterinary appointment.

cost.label: Budget
cost.heading: Cost of Ownership
cost.html:
Most Greyhounds are adopted through rescue at $250–$450, which typically includes spay/neuter, vaccinations, heartworm test, and a basic health check. Breeder puppies (show/companion lines) run $1,500–$2,500 but are much less common. Dental care is the primary ongoing health cost to budget for.

right_for_you.label: Fit Assessment
right_for_you.heading: Is a Greyhound Right for You?

Live in an apartment or home without a big yard
Open to adopting an adult dog from a racing rescue
Appreciate a gentle, quiet, dignified companion
Can commit to dental care and safe fencing
not_fit: You have a small apartment without nearby outdoor space — at 60–70 lbs, Greyhounds need room to stretch and a routine of off-property exercise

You expect a calm, quiet first 8-12 weeks — Greyhound puppies, like all breeds, go through a 'puppy blues' phase of sleep loss, biting, accidents, and overwhelm that 73% of new sole-caretakers report struggling with
Want a dog you can let off-leash in an open area
Have small pets (cats, rabbits) without careful introduction
Want an enthusiastically obedient, high-energy working partner
Can't provide adequate soft bedding and winter warmth
Need a dog comfortable with rough handling or loud environments

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Finding Your Greyhound
finding.html:
Adoption from Racing Rescue

The vast majority of Greyhound adoptions come through National Greyhound Adoption Program (NGAP), Greyhound Pets of America (GPA), and regional rescue groups. Adoption fees of $250–$450 typically include neuter/spay, vaccinations, heartworm treatment if needed, and a health exam. These organizations also assess each dog's compatibility with cats and children before placement — which matters a lot with a breed that has a strong prey drive.

Buying from a Breeder

Companion-bred (non-racing) Greyhound puppies do exist but are uncommon. Expect $1,500–$2,500 and a wait. The Greyhound Club of America can provide referrals. Health testing expectations include cardiac evaluation and thyroid testing. For most people, rescue is the better path — you get an adult dog with a known personality, already past the chaotic puppy stage.

Before you put down a deposit, go through the Greyhound puppy checklist — it covers what to have ready before they arrive.

faq.a: Yes — they're genuinely excellent apartment dogs despite their size, which surprises almost everyone. They sleep 16–18 hours a day, don't bark much, and don't pace or need constant stimulation. The main requirement is two decent walks a day and access to a securely fenced area for occasional sprinting. No yard required.

Two reasons: prey drive and speed. When a Greyhound sees something move — a squirrel, a cyclist, a distant dog — a hardwired chase response activates. At 45 mph, they're across a road and out of sight in seconds. There's no reliably training this away in an uncontrolled environment. Every Greyhound owner will tell you this is the one absolute rule: leash or fence, always. It's not negotiable.

Generally yes, with some considerations. They're gentle and not aggressive, but they're sensitive and can be overwhelmed by very loud or chaotic young children. They also move fast enough to knock over a toddler by accident. With school-age kids who've been taught to interact calmly, they're typically excellent. Very young children require supervision and taught boundaries.

Greyhounds lack the body fat that other dogs use to metabolize barbiturate-based anesthetics (like thiopental), which means standard doses can be fatal. They also have different liver enzyme levels. Any vet treating your Greyhound must know this — most sighthound-aware vets use propofol-based protocols instead. Carry a card in your dog's vet file and mention it at every appointment, including emergencies.
